properties.name: add_epoch and plan_epoch take a description, add_requirement takes a priority — the two fields a user reported, answered
properties.rationale:
This is the change that answers the report. The two before it - making the class visible and gating it - are worth having and neither of them would have changed anything for the person who wrote the feedback, which is the over-engineering pattern this project's owner watches for by name. A user said two fields were missing; the smallest honest answer is to add them.

THE MOVED PIN IS THE EVIDENCE. The reachability test asserted both properties WERE reported as unreachable; that assertion now reads the other way and was observed failing in the old direction before the parameters landed. A pin that moves with a fix, rather than being deleted by it, is what keeps a fix from being asserted rather than shown.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
The dev_storyflow agent reported on 2026-09-07 that add_epoch had no description and add_requirement no priority. Neither was ever lost: both properties have been declared since their types existed and no typed tool ever offered them. This gives them parameters.

DesignEpoch.description is that type's EMBEDDING FIELD, so the field search_design finds an epoch BY could not be written by the tool that makes one, and the reporter's workaround was to put a paragraph into `name`. Both add_epoch and plan_epoch take it, through one shared helper, because a fix put in one of that pair and not the other is exactly how the sequence-hint defect recurred on the sibling the next day.

Requirement.priority declares `default: medium` and the default is injected at write, so every requirement carried a priority nobody chose and nobody could change through the surface: 193 of 207 sat at the injected value and the 14 that did not came through the generic escape hatch. Omitting the parameter still leaves the default, which is unchanged behaviour - the parameter adds a way to SAY, not an obligation to. Its legal values are published from the schema, and an undeclared value is refused with the set named.

FAILING FIRST, OBSERVED: the four tests were written before the parameters and three failed with the serde refusals verbatim - "unknown field `priority`, expected one of id, name, statement, distinct_from, status, approver, acted_at" and "unknown field `description`, expected one of id, name, epoch_type, sequence". All four pass now. They pin that the value reaches the STORED PROPERTY, not merely that the call is accepted, because a tool that takes a field and drops it passes a signature check and still fails the caller.

AND THE INSTRUMENT CAUGHT A DEFECT IN ITSELF, SAME DAY IT SHIPPED. Adding one parameter made SIX properties read as newly reachable instead of two. Cause: the tool-to-type map held only the `add_*` constructors, so plan_epoch, every setter and link_artifact were pooled as cross-type and their parameter names leaked to every type - the identical cross-type leak the map was added to stop, one tool-family along. Two fixes: the map now covers every tool that writes a type's own properties, and READ-ONLY TOOLS ARE EXCLUDED ENTIRELY, because a read cannot write anything and seven read tools were being counted as writers on the strength of parameter names like `limit` and `query` that happen to match property names.

WITH THE LEAK CLOSED THE GATE IMMEDIATELY REPORTED FIVE MORE REAL HOLES the leak had been hiding: Actor.description, Interface.description, Release.description, Resource.description and DesignEpoch.checksum. They are pre-existing, not regressions, and are grandfathered into the baseline rather than fixed here - four of them are the same one-line fix as the epoch's, and that is a scope decision for the owner rather than one to take while passing.
